title: Meaning in Pain
question: Viktor Frankl argued that even in unavoidable suffering a person can still find what?
correctExplanation: Yes. Frankl held that hardship can be borne when it carries meaning, a lesson drawn from the camps.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is meaning in suffering. The pain cannot always be removed, but the attitude toward it can still hold purpose.
lessonContent:
Some hardship cannot be removed.
What remains is the stance one takes.
Meaning can lighten what cannot be changed.
Attitude is the final variable.
Share this: find one unavoidable difficulty and name what it can teach.

title: Healing Through Meaning
question: What is the name of the school of therapy founded by Viktor Frankl?
correctExplanation: Yes. Its name points to healing through a focus on meaning and purpose.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is logotherapy. It centres on the human need for purpose rather than drive or conditioning alone.
lessonContent:
Approaches to healing differ in their focus.
One school centres on purpose.
Meaning can be a therapeutic aim.
Treat the whole person, not just symptoms.
Share this: consider what gives one of your hard days a purpose.

title: Drive for Purpose
question: Frankl described a primary human drive beyond pleasure and power. What did he call it?
correctExplanation: Yes. He placed the pursuit of purpose alongside or above other drives.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the will to meaning. People endure great difficulty for a purpose, which pleasure alone cannot explain.
lessonContent:
Motives go beyond comfort and control.
Purpose can outrank pleasure.
People endure for what matters to them.
Ask what a person is living for.
Share this: name what makes one of your efforts worth it.

title: Empty Feeling
question: Frankl used what term for the emptiness people feel when life seems to lack purpose?
correctExplanation: Yes. The image is an inner emptiness that boredom and restlessness often fill.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is an existential vacuum. When purpose is missing, people may chase distraction to escape the emptiness.
lessonContent:
Absence of purpose has a felt shape.
Emptiness invites distraction.
Boredom can signal a missing aim.
Name the void before filling it.
Share this: notice one distraction you use to avoid an emptiness.

title: Hope and Hardship
question: What did Frankl call the stance that stays hopeful while fully acknowledging life's pain?
correctExplanation: Yes. It accepts suffering honestly while still affirming that life can be worthwhile.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is tragic optimism. It is not denial but hope that has looked hardship in the face.
lessonContent:
Hope need not ignore pain.
Realism and optimism can coexist.
Acknowledge the worst while staying open.
Avoid both denial and despair.
Share this: hold one hard fact and one hope together today.

title: Values of Attitude
question: Frankl named one source of meaning as the stance taken toward an unchangeable fate. Which value is that?
correctExplanation: Yes. When circumstances cannot change, the attitude chosen becomes a source of meaning.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is attitudinal values. They matter most precisely when nothing else can be altered.
lessonContent:
Some sources of meaning lie in response, not circumstance.
Attitude can be chosen when events cannot.
Dignity survives the loss of control.
Look to the stance you can still take.
Share this: name one fixed situation and the stance you choose toward it.

title: Values of Creation
question: Which Frankl value names meaning found through making or contributing something?
correctExplanation: Yes. Work and creation give life meaning by adding something to the world.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is creative values. Contribution turns effort into a lasting source of purpose.
lessonContent:
Making things gives life shape.
Contribution connects effort to others.
Work can be more than a wage.
Create something that outlasts the day.
Share this: note one thing you made this week and what it meant.

title: Values of Experience
question: Which Frankl value names meaning found through encountering beauty, truth, or another person?
correctExplanation: Yes. Meaning can arrive through what we receive, not only through what we do.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is experiential values. Love and beauty enrich life without requiring any achievement.
lessonContent:
Meaning can be received, not only produced.
Beauty and connection nourish purpose.
Some value arrives without effort.
Be present to what enriches you.
Share this: notice one experience this week that felt deeply worthwhile.

title: Final Freedom
question: Frankl wrote that the last of the human freedoms is the ability to choose what?
correctExplanation: Yes. Even when everything external is stripped away, the inner response remains a person's own.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the last freedom. Circumstances can remove almost everything except the choice of response.
lessonContent:
External control has limits.
The response to events remains personal.
Freedom can survive constraint.
Protect the inner choice.
Share this: identify one response that is entirely yours to choose.

title: Choosing Response
question: For Frankl, what can a person always decide even when circumstances are fixed?
correctExplanation: Yes. The stance taken toward unchangeable conditions is the freedom that cannot be taken away.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is choosing one's attitude. Events may be forced, but the response to them remains a choice.
lessonContent:
Response is not the same as circumstance.
Some freedom survives every constraint.
Attitude is a decision point.
Exercise it deliberately.
Share this: choose one deliberate response to a fixed annoyance today.

title: Answer to Life
question: Frankl said meaning is not invented but expressed through what quality toward life's demands?
correctExplanation: Yes. Life asks questions of us, and meaning lies in how we answer them.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is responsibleness. Each unique situation makes a demand to which we must respond.
lessonContent:
Meaning can be a response, not an invention.
Each situation asks something of us.
Answer with what the moment needs.
Take ownership of your reply.
Share this: ask what one current situation is asking of you.

title: Spiritual Dimension
question: Frankl named the uniquely human dimension of freedom and meaning by what term?
correctExplanation: Yes. He set this dimension apart from the bodily and psychological, as the home of will and meaning.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is noetic dimension. It is the distinctly human capacity to take a stance toward oneself.
lessonContent:
Views of a person may be layered.
One layer holds will and meaning.
Distinguish capacities from drives.
Human freedom has its own domain.
Share this: notice a moment when you took a stance toward yourself.

title: Weekend Emptiness
question: Frankl used what phrase for the distress that surfaces when the week's routine stops?
correctExplanation: Yes. The phrase names the emptiness that appears when busyness no longer fills the hours.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is Sunday neurosis. Once work stops, people may feel a void they normally avoid.
lessonContent:
Busyness can mask a missing purpose.
Idle hours expose what work hides.
Symptoms can point to meaning, not illness.
Listen to what the quiet reveals.
Share this: notice what arises when your schedule empties.

title: Reverse Intention
question: Frankl devised a technique that asks a patient to intend the very thing they fear. What is it called?
correctExplanation: Yes. By aiming at the feared outcome, the patient loosens the grip of anxiety.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is paradoxical intention. Facing the fear on purpose removes the pressure that feeds it.
lessonContent:
Fighting a symptom can strengthen it.
Approaching it deliberately can disarm it.
Reverse the goal to break a loop.
Reduce the stakes of the feared thing.
Share this: imagine your small fear in a lighter, humorous way.

title: Turning Outward
question: Frankl advised patients to stop watching themselves and look outward instead. What technique is this?
correctExplanation: Yes. Shifting attention away from oneself reduces the intensifying effect of self-monitoring.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is dereflection. Over-attention can inflame a problem, so turning outward brings relief.
lessonContent:
Self-focus can magnify discomfort.
Attention outward can loosen symptoms.
Some cures come from forgetting oneself.
Redirect, rather than struggle.
Share this: spend one hour absorbed in something outside yourself.

title: Through Work
question: Frankl listed three main paths to meaning. One is found in what everyday activity?
correctExplanation: Yes. Doing something that matters to others is one of his three broad routes to purpose.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is meaning through work. Contribution through tasks is a daily source of purpose.
lessonContent:
Purpose has more than one avenue.
One route runs through effort.
Work can serve others.
Connect the task to its recipients.
Share this: trace one task to the person it helps.

title: Through Love
question: Frankl named encountering another person deeply as another path to meaning. What is it?
correctExplanation: Yes. Genuine connection with another person opens a distinct source of value.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is meaning through love. Relationship reveals uniqueness in another that no achievement can replace.
lessonContent:
Connection offers its own kind of purpose.
Another person reveals unique value.
Presence can matter more than output.
Attend fully to those you care for.
Share this: give one person your undivided attention today.

title: Through Courage
question: The third Frankl path is the stance taken toward unavoidable difficulty. What does it take?
correctExplanation: Yes. Facing what cannot be changed with dignity is itself a way of finding purpose.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is meaning through courage. When fate is fixed, the bearing of it becomes the source of worth.
lessonContent:
Some situations demand a response, not a fix.
Bearing hardship well is its own achievement.
Dignity does not require success.
Meet what cannot change with resolve.
Share this: meet one unavoidable burden with deliberate dignity.

title: A Reason to Live
question: Frankl quoted the idea that a person can endure almost any how if they have what?
correctExplanation: Yes. A compelling purpose can carry a person through enormous difficulty.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the why to live. The reason for enduring matters as much as the capacity to endure.
lessonContent:
Purpose strengthens endurance.
A reason makes hardship bearable.
Know what you are living toward.
Anchor effort to that aim.
Share this: write one sentence on what you are living toward.

title: Beyond the Self
question: Frankl said meaning is found not by self-absorption but by pointing toward what?
correctExplanation: Yes. Purpose tends to come from serving something larger than one's own concerns.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is self-transcendence. Meaning often appears when attention moves beyond the self toward a cause or person.
lessonContent:
Purpose rarely grows from self-focus.
Devotion to something larger brings meaning.
Look outward to find footing.
Serve beyond your own concerns.
Share this: commit one act in service of something larger than you.

title: Freedom Within
question: What did Frankl say could not be taken from a person even in the worst conditions?
correctExplanation: Yes. The capacity to choose one's stance survived even total external deprivation.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is inner freedom. External power can constrain the body but not fully own the mind's response.
lessonContent:
Some freedoms are not granted by circumstance.
The inner life can resist external control.
Hold the ground you still command.
Exercise it daily to keep it.
Share this: name one inner choice no one else can make for you.

title: Meaning of the Moment
question: For Frankl, meaning is not a vague general aim but something found in what?
correctExplanation: Yes. Each concrete situation carries a specific demand, not a single life-long formula.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the meaning of the moment. Purpose is discovered in particular circumstances rather than an abstract plan.
lessonContent:
Purpose is concrete, not abstract.
Each situation makes its own demand.
Attend to what this moment asks.
Avoid waiting for a grand plan.
Share this: ask what the next hour is asking of you.

title: Meaning Without Conditions
question: Frankl insisted that the possibility of meaning exists under what conditions?
correctExplanation: Yes. He held that life retains meaning even when health, freedom, and comfort are gone.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is unconditional meaning. Purpose is not contingent on favourable circumstances.
lessonContent:
Meaning need not wait for better conditions.
Even deprivation leaves room for purpose.
Avoid tying worth to comfort.
Look for meaning where you are.
Share this: find one source of meaning that circumstance cannot remove.

title: Why Keep Going
question: Frankl observed that those who survived often shared what kind of possession?
correctExplanation: Yes. Survivors often held a task or a person awaiting them, which gave the strength to continue.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a reason to endure. Purpose can be a literal life raft when conditions are unbearable.
lessonContent:
Purpose can sustain survival.
A waiting task gives strength.
Hold something ahead of you.
Meaning is practical, not decorative.
Share this: name what you are enduring toward.

title: The Search Goes On
question: Frankl taught that meaning is not a final answer but a continuing what?
correctExplanation: Yes. Meaning is pursued across changing circumstances rather than settled once and for all.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the search continues. Purpose is a sustained practice, not a single discovery.
lessonContent:
Meaning is a practice, not a trophy.
Circumstances change what purpose demands.
Keep asking the question.
Expect it to evolve over time.
Share this: revisit what gives your life meaning once this month.
